title: A Man Was Sleeping With His Father’s Wife—and the Corinthian Church Was Proud
paragraphs:
A Man Was Sleeping With His Father’s Wife—and the Corinthian Church Was Proud
The scandal in Corinth was horrifying. But what should terrify us even more is that Paul was not only confronting the man in sin—he was confronting a church that had learned how to tolerate what should have broken its heart.
There are Bible passages we love to underline.
And then there are Bible passages we quietly wish were not there.
First Corinthians 5 is one of them.
It does not begin with a miracle.
It does not begin with an inspirational promise.
It begins with a scandal.
A sexual scandal.
Inside a church.
And somehow, the most disturbing part of the story is not simply what one man was doing behind closed doors.
It is what the church was doing in public.
They were proud.
Paul had heard what was happening in Corinth, and when he addressed it, he did not soften the language to protect anyone's comfort:
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife.”
—1 Corinthians 5:1, ESV
The Greek is even more revealing.
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
Literally, the opening carries the force of something like:
“Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you…”
The word Paul uses is πορνεία — porneia.
It refers broadly to sexual immorality—sexual behavior outside the boundaries established by God.
Paul was not describing gossip.
He was not talking about a misunderstanding.
He was confronting an ongoing sexual relationship so scandalous that he says even the surrounding Gentile culture did not ordinarily tolerate it.
A man had his father’s wife.

Most interpreters understand Paul to mean the man's stepmother rather than his biological mother, particularly because Paul says “his father’s wife.” The language also echoes the Old Testament prohibition against uncovering one's father's nakedness by taking his wife.
Leviticus 18:8 says:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife; it is your father’s nakedness.”
This was not merely socially awkward.
It was rebellion against God's revealed sexual boundaries.
But then Paul says something that should stop every Christian who has ever learned to become comfortable around unrepentant sin.
“And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?”
—1 Corinthians 5:2, ESV
The Greek is devastating:
καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ
Kai hymeis pephysiōmenoi este.
“And you are puffed up.”
Inflated.
Swollen with pride.
Paul expected grief.
He found arrogance.
He expected mourning.
He found boasting.
He expected a church brokenhearted that someone bearing the name of Christ was openly living contrary to Christ.
Instead, something had happened to their conscience.
They had apparently learned how to coexist with scandal without mourning it.
And suddenly this ancient Corinthian church does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Because there is a terrifying stage in spiritual decline when sin no longer shocks us.
Then comes another stage when it no longer grieves us.
And eventually, if we are not careful, we begin finding sophisticated reasons to defend what Scripture tells us to repent of.
That is when Corinth stops being merely a city on an ancient map.
Corinth becomes a mirror.
And perhaps that is why this chapter makes us uncomfortable.
It is easier to stare at the unnamed man than to let Scripture stare back at us.
We can read about his sexual immorality and think:
How could he?
But Paul turns toward the congregation and essentially asks:
How could you become comfortable with it?
That question reaches beyond sexual sin.
How did bitterness become normal in your heart?
How did secret pornography become something you manage instead of something you bring into the light?
How did dishonesty become “just business”?
How did hatred become “discernment”?
How did gossip become “concern”?
How did unforgiveness become “boundaries” when, deep down, you know you are feeding resentment?
How did pride become confidence?
How did greed become ambition?
How did prayerlessness become busyness?
How did months pass without opening your Bible while you continued telling everyone that you were “just going through a season”?
How did you become able to sing about holiness on Sunday while protecting the very thing Jesus has been asking you to surrender?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the person sitting beside you at church would never imagine it.
But God knows.
And strangely enough, that should not merely terrify you.
For the repentant sinner, it should give you hope.
Because the God who sees what you are hiding is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Paul's response in Corinth was severe because sin is severe.
He instructed the church to remove this persistently immoral professing believer from their fellowship.
That sounds harsh to modern ears until we understand the purpose.
Paul writes that such a person was to be handed over “for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.”
The goal was not cruelty.
The goal was restoration.
The discipline was meant to destroy the illusion that someone could cling defiantly to sin while enjoying all the assurances of Christian fellowship as though nothing were wrong.
Biblical love does not smile while someone walks toward destruction.
Biblical love tells the truth.
But biblical truth does not end with condemnation either.
This is where the story becomes astonishing.
Because when many Christians hear “church discipline,” they imagine permanent exile.
God's purpose is different.
Correction aims toward repentance.
Repentance opens the door toward restoration.
And there is a fascinating connection many interpreters have seen between 1 Corinthians and Paul's later words in 2 Corinthians.

We should be careful here: Scripture does not explicitly identify the repentant person in 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 as the same man from 1 Corinthians 5. Many interpreters have proposed that connection, while others believe Paul was referring to a different offender.
But regardless of the man's exact identity, Paul's theology of restoration could not be clearer.
When discipline has produced repentance, Paul does not tell Christians to keep crushing the sinner.
He says:
“You should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.”
—2 Corinthians 2:7, ESV
Read that again.
Forgive him.
Comfort him.
Then Paul says:
“So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.”
—2 Corinthians 2:8, ESV
This is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not redefining rebellion until repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not humiliating broken people forever because their worst chapter became public.
Truth confronts.
Grace restores.
The cross explains why both are necessary.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
Jesus died because sin was deadly.
And Jesus did not rise because sinners were beyond redemption.
He rose because death itself would not have the final word over everyone united to Him.
That changes how we read Corinth.
The Gospel is not:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel is not:
“Try harder so God will finally tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that the holy God against whom we have sinned came near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Christ lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose bodily from the grave.
Forgiveness therefore is not God pretending your rebellion never happened.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
Grace is free to us because it was costly to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years misunderstanding grace.
You thought grace meant God would leave you alone.
But grace loves you too much for that.
Paul later asks the Corinthians:
“Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?”
Then he names sins.
Sexual immorality.
Idolatry.
Adultery.
Theft.
Greed.
Drunkenness.
Reviling.
Swindling.
And then comes one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to a scandal-filled church:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Not because they had never committed those sins.
They had.
Not because their histories had somehow become respectable.
They had not.
But something happened.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV
That is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed.
Such were some of you.
Your past can describe where Christ found you without determining where Christ is taking you.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Liar.
Pornography-bound.
Greedy.
Bitter.
Proud.
Drunk.
Sexually broken.
Religiously hypocritical.
Secretly exhausted.
Spiritually numb.
Ashamed.
The Gospel does not require you to manufacture a cleaner history.
Jesus specializes in resurrecting people who finally stop pretending they are alive.
But do not confuse grace with permission.
Jesus does not merely forgive us in our sin.
He begins freeing us from its dominion.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
You cannot purchase the blood of Christ with tears.
You cannot earn justification by cleaning yourself up.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But genuine grace changes direction.
The New Testament word often translated “repentance,” μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of a change of mind that involves a transformed orientation toward God and sin.
Repentance says:
“I cannot keep calling good what God calls evil.”
“I cannot keep hiding.”
“I cannot keep blaming everyone else.”
“I cannot keep asking Jesus to save me while demanding that my favorite idol remain untouched.”
Maybe your Corinth is a browser history.
Maybe it is an affair nobody has discovered.
Maybe it is the person you cannot forgive.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is the image you maintain online.
Maybe it is your private messages.
Maybe it is envy.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe your scandal has never appeared publicly.
But heaven does not need screenshots.
God already sees it.
And still—
Christ calls you.
That is what makes grace almost unbearable in its beauty.
Jesus already knew the ugliest truth about you when He called sinners to Himself.
You cannot shock an omniscient Savior.
You cannot reveal something in confession that God only discovered when you finally admitted it.
Repentance is not informing God.
It is agreeing with Him.
And confession is not crawling toward a reluctant Christ who must somehow be persuaded to show mercy.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, ESV
Maybe this article is your moment.
Not because these words are magical.
They are not.
But perhaps the Word of God has put its finger on something you have been protecting.
There is a kind of pain that destroys you.
And there is a kind of pain that finally makes you stop touching the thing that has been destroying you.
Bring it to Jesus.
Name it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
If another person is being harmed, stop the harm.
If accountability is needed, seek it.
If you need your pastor or mature believers around you, tell them.
If your situation involves abuse, coercion, exploitation, or danger, seek appropriate professional and lawful help rather than treating the matter as merely a private spiritual struggle.
Come into the light.
Not because Christians never fall.
But because people being transformed by Christ cannot make peace with darkness forever.
And Christian, when another believer genuinely repents, remember Corinth from the other direction too.
Do not become the person who loves exposing sin more than seeing sinners restored.
Some Christians know how to discipline but have forgotten how to forgive.
They know someone's scandal from ten years ago better than they know the evidence of God's grace in that person's life today.
But if heaven rejoices over repentance, why would we resent restoration?
The cross leaves no room for moral superiority.
Every redeemed person stands at Calvary with empty hands.
There are no VIP sections beneath the blood of Jesus.
Only sinners.
Only grace.
Only a Savior worthy of all the glory.
Maybe that is why the Corinthian scandal still matters.
It forces us to hold two truths together that our culture constantly tries to separate.
Sin is worse than we want to admit.
And Jesus is more merciful than we dared to hope.
Take away the first truth and grace becomes cheap sentimentality.
Take away the second and Christianity becomes hopeless condemnation.
At the cross, both truths meet.
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
His grace is powerful enough to rewrite what sin tried to make your final chapter.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this message:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner.
Not by renaming darkness.
By bringing us into light.
Not by telling guilty people that holiness no longer matters.
By washing, sanctifying, justifying, restoring, and transforming people through the Gospel.
So be honest.
What did this expose?
If there is something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your sin for strangers to inspect. But you can stop pretending.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes three words are enough to say, I don't want to fight alone anymore.
Then look around the comments.
Remember that behind those names are real human beings fighting battles you may know nothing about.
Pray for one another.
Encourage repentance rather than humiliation.
Point one another toward Jesus.
And if one person came to mind while you were reading this, send this article to them personally.
Not as an accusation.
Not with, “This is about you.”
Send it with love.
It hasn't.

Supporting Gospel work financially is not what saves you, proves your salvation, or purchases God's blessing. Christ alone saves, and Christians glorify God in many forms of faithful obedience. But voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way believers participate in Gospel ministry.
More importantly, your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered resources designed to call people away from darkness and toward Jesus Christ.
Not to prove anything to God.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
And before you leave, remember this:
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the feet of Jesus—but once grace takes hold of you, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
